t: Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066, and Harold had to face three rival claimants, Hardrada and Tostig in the north and William in the south, within a few weeks.
The English fought on foot in a shield wall; the Normans used archers, infantry and cavalry, and probably pretended to flee in order to break the English line.
The battle is known from conflicting accounts, so that even Harold's death, by an arrow in the eye in the traditional version, remains uncertain.
dyk: Although later lists of William's companions exist, only about 35 named individuals can reliably be identified as having been with him at Hastings, and only about 20 named Englishmen with Harold.
ev: Edward the Confessor dies on 5 January; Harold Godwinson is elected and crowned king
Harald Hardrada and Tostig defeat an English army at Fulford on 20 September
Harold defeats the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge on 25 September, and Hardrada and Tostig are killed
William lands at Pevensey on 28 September and builds a wooden castle at Hastings
Harold camps at Caldbec Hill on the night of 13 October
On 14 October the battle is fought from about 9 am to dusk, and Harold is killed
William marches on London, receives the English leaders' surrender at Berkhamsted and is crowned on 25 December
William puts down risings in the north and west, culminating in the Harrying of the North into 1070

f.date: Saturday 14 October 1066, from about 9 am to dusk
f.place: About 7 miles (11 km) northwest of Hastings, close to the present-day town of Battle, East Sussex, England; sources differ on the exact site of the English line
f.sides: A Norman-French army under William, Duke of Normandy, against an English army under King Harold Godwinson; numbers unknown, with modern estimates of 7000 to 8000 for the Normans among several, and most historians arguing for 7000 to 8000 English
f.outcome: Harold was killed late in the battle, most of his army retreated or was defeated, and William went on to be crowned king of England on 25 December 1066.
